Recent research supports separating persistent preferences from recent intent and learning their relative importance. [TLSTSRec (2024/2025)](https://doi.org/10.3233/ida-240051) combines temporal representations with adaptive long/short-term fusion. [HM4SR (WWW 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14269) introduces interactive and temporal mixtures of experts, explicit timestamp embeddings, and auxiliary contrastive objectives targeting sparsity. Its multimodal inputs and category-prediction supervision exceed this benchmark’s available data; temporal routing and ID-based contrastive learning are transferable hypotheses.

Two 2026 directions sharpen the design. [MGUI](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11506283) combines time-interval gating for individual recent items, group-level interest modeling, cross-user transition graphs, and user-specific expert weighting. [MIMAR-SRec (AAAI 2026)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38489) models intent across contextual windows, with contrastive alignment and robustness against interaction, temporal, and preference noise. These papers motivate multiple temporal views, but do not establish gains on the pinned RecHarness evaluation.

A practical experiment inferred from these approaches: retain SASRec, add pooled historical-interest and recent-window branches, then gate their contributions using sequence length, observed time gaps, and branch representations. Compare fixed fusion, learned fusion, and timestamp-conditioned fusion; inspect performance by history length and gap size, alongside expert utilization. Start with a small gate because sparse histories provide limited routing evidence. Treat inferred intent transitions, satisfied needs, and compatibility as latent hypotheses—not observed labels—and select changes solely by macro validation HR@10.
